newsitem.title: UK: China the wild card in turbulent world zinc.
newsitem.headline: China the wild card in turbulent world zinc.

text.p: LME zinc continues to gyrate wildly between the poles of Chinese borrowing and short covering, speculative buying and fund profit- taking.
Concern has focused on the short Chinese position, which has been partially covered and the rest rolled over, several metals analysts said on Thursday.
"The Chinese have tried to spread the risk by exchanging 3-months zinc commitments for contracts based on the annual average for 1998," one said.

A residual short position still exists, and this may account for the firm cash-threes spread, but the majority of 250,000 tonnes the Chinese were due to deliver in September has been covered or rolled forward, according to these analysts and LME traders.
They said that by using futures and options to delay squaring up their positions, the Chinese smelters were setting themselves up for future squeezes and further losses.
The strategy of buying call options with a strike price of $1,450-$1,650 to lock in losses had also failed to extricate the Chinese from their predicament, analysts said.

Comments by the Chinese zinc industry during the recent turmoil in zinc have been seen as contradictory. But the analysts saw this as the result of ill-conceived trading strategies rather than an attempt to manipulate price levels, although increased prices have brought higher revenues in Chinese physical trade.
"It did not make sense for a net exporter to talk down the market by announcing increases in production unless they had over-committed themselves," an analyst said.
Traders said they were "mystified" by the situation. "It is very difficult to know what to believe in terms of what comes out of China," said a trader.
"The zinc market has been a wild old beast. These moves have done a lot of damage to the market," a London trader said.

Zinc traded to a low of $1,410 early on Thursday before bouncing back to over $1,450 and spreads remained firm at around $90. Dealers remained cautious and the market is expected to continue volatile.
Analysts said that trade had been "thin and nervous" in a range of almost $100 on Wednesday.
Investor interest was two-way on Thursday, with long liquidation offset by speculative buying, traders said.
Alan Williamson of Bain and Co said zinc was likely to find a range of $1,350-$1,400. "Anything above $1,400 during the summer slowdown is just a bit of a bubble," he added.
"In the short term zinc is likely to remain volatile with a bias for the upside," said Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff.
LME brokers Brandeis pegged resistance at $1,547 and support at $1,420.
Asian traders and Chinese industry sources said on Thursday they expected prices to stabilise around $1,400 to $1,450 a tonne, or even drop lower in the immediate term.
"It should drop from here, I think $1,400 or below would be more reasonable," a Chinese metals industry executive said.

"I don't think it will go ballistic again; it is happy around here between $1,400-1,450," the Singapore trader said, though he added: "It all depends on the funds, it could be at $2,000 by the end of the year."

Fundamentals, including falling world stocks, rising demand on good world-wide economic growth, and increasing production of galvanized steel, had long pointed to rises in the zinc price to about $1,450 a tonne, analysts have said.
But the signals were either missed or misinterpreted by Chinese metals industry leaders, who in late 1996 directed smelters to sell forward once the price reached levels around $1,100.
And sell forward they did, to the tune of about 200,000 to 250,000 tonnes, according to sources in Beijing's metals production arm China National Nonferrous Metals Corp (CNNC).
Some Chinese forward selling had been done at $1,280 and $1,350, one source said.
The turbulence in zinc has also impacted on the other base metals, in particular copper and aluminium.

Traders said that copper was "ominously quiet" early on Thursday, and with a contraction in the backwardation to around $30, traders said they expected a price slide to $2,200, from $2,300 on Thursday.
Aluminium remains firm, and is seen rising to $1,800 if the market can consolidate above $1,717, said analysts.
"There is good buying, I think prices will go higher," a trader said.
Analysts warned that a squeeze in aluminium may be unsuccessful once off-exchange stocks come into play.
"Volatility in any one market does create nervousness across the board," a trader said. -- London Newsroom + 44 171 542 8071
